hops.title: The polywater scare and a sweaty T-shirt
hops.text: In the 1960s, chemists found a strange liquid inside glass tubes as thin as a hair. It was syrupy, froze at minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit and boiled near 400. Some feared this "polywater" might spread and change ordinary water. Then Bell Labs physicist Denis Rousseau played a hard game of handball, wrung sweat from his T-shirt and tested its chemical fingerprint. It closely matched polywater. Polywater turned out to be ordinary water loaded with impurities, and sweat was one clue to where they came from.

sources.citation: Ramirez A. The Rise and Fall of Polywater. Distillations, Science History Institute (2020).
Rousseau DL. "Polywater" and sweat: similarities between the infrared spectra. Science 171(3967):170-172 (1971); Ramirez A, Science History Institute (2020).

image.caption: The famous "new water" was ordinary water loaded with impurities, and a sweaty shirt helped show it.

hops.title: Why water is a weak fix for a spicy chili
hops.text: When a chili pepper sets your mouth on fire, the usual move is to gulp water. It helps, but less than milk does. Capsaicin, the chemical behind the burn, is mostly water-repelling, so it dissolves poorly in water. Penn State researchers gave 72 volunteers spicy tomato juice, then tested seven drinks, water included. Chilled whole milk and chilled skim milk both eased the burn more than room-temperature water did. That hints that something in milk, perhaps its protein, may grab capsaicin; the study did not test this.

sources.citation: Nolden AA, Lenart G, Hayes JE. Putting out the fire - Efficacy of common beverages in reducing oral burn from capsaicin. Physiology & Behavior 208:112557 (2019).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A teenager fanning their mouth at a kitchen table with a red chili pepper, a glass of water and a half-empty glass of milk.
image.caption: Capsaicin dissolves poorly in water. In the study, chilled milk eased the burn more than room-temperature water.

hops.afterHeading: Explain: why the Bay barely warmed
hops.title: Water-cooled underwear inside a spacesuit
hops.text: Spacewalkers face temperatures up to 250 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sunlight, and their own body heat builds up inside the sealed suit. So the first thing an astronaut pulls on is stretchy spandex long underwear threaded with about 300 feet of thin tubes. A pump and chiller in the backpack send cold water through the tubes, right next to the skin. Water suits the job because of its high specific heat: each gram soaks up a lot of body heat while warming only a little, then carries it away.

sources.citation: NASA Johnson Space Center. Spacewalk Spacesuit Basics (2019).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A stretchy white spacesuit undergarment threaded with loops of thin blue water-filled tubing next to a spacesuit helmet.
image.caption: Water's high specific heat lets chilled water in thin tubes carry a spacewalker's body heat away.

audio.title: Lapping cats, sweaty water and seals that take the ocean's temperature
audio.transcript:
Here are three places where water's slightly charged ends quietly run the show.

First, watch a cat drink from a bowl. Dogs look as if they scoop water with a curled tongue, but X-ray videos show they lift it the same basic way cats do. But a dog plunges its tongue into the water and yanks it up much faster, so its column is bigger and splashier. Using high-speed cameras, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Virginia Tech and Princeton found that a house cat curls the tip of its tongue backward, so only the smooth top barely brushes the surface. Water sticks to the tongue by adhesion, and as the cat snaps its tongue straight up, a neat column of water rises right behind it. The cat shuts its jaws in the split second before gravity pulls the column back down, and its chin stays dry. House cats do this about four times a second. The team also slowed down zoo footage and online videos of lions, tigers and jaguars, and found that big cats appear to use the same mechanism, at a slower beat to match their bigger tongues.

Second, meet the super-water scare of the nineteen sixties. A few chemists condensed water inside glass tubes as thin as a human hair and got a strange, syrupy liquid. It froze at minus forty degrees Fahrenheit and did not boil until nearly four hundred. Some scientists thought ordinary water molecules had snapped into permanent honeycomb chains. They called it polywater, and some worried it might spread and change ordinary water. Then Bell Labs physicist Denis Rousseau went to the gym. After a hard game of handball, he wrung the sweat out of his shirt and checked its chemical fingerprint. It looked a lot like polywater's. Both looked remarkably like sodium lactate, a compound found in sweat. He published the result in nineteen seventy-one. Water had never turned into a monster chain at all. Chemical tests found high concentrations of impurities in the tiny samples, enough to explain their strange behavior.

Finally, zoom out from one buoy in the Chesapeake Bay to the whole planet. Water covers more than seventy percent of Earth, and each gram takes a lot of energy to warm, so the oceans act like a gigantic heat sponge. According to federal ocean scientists, the sea has absorbed an estimated ninety-one percent of the extra heat trapped in Earth's climate system by excess greenhouse gases, and waves and currents mix much of that warmth downward. Tracking all that stored heat takes some creative helpers. Alongside satellites and ships, scientists keep a fleet of more than three thousand robotic floats that drift deep underwater and bob to the surface about every ten days to beam their temperatures home. And in waters that are hard to reach by ship, researchers have fitted seals with temperature instruments. Seal-borne sensors add readings from places a ship cannot easily go. The Bay buoy showed how little the water's temperature changed in one day. Across the oceans, floats, ships and even seals help scientists track how much heat the water has stored.
